primary_cause: Collapsing oil-demand expectations plus OPEC+ uncertainty. IEA said Q1 oil demand would fall YoY for first time since 2009
secondary_factors: OPEC seeking additional 1.5M bpd production cut at Mar 5-6 Vienna meeting while Russia had not yet agreed. General equity risk-off
store_description: Exxon's drop was macro and commodity-driven not tied to a fresh company event. By March 5 investors were processing the prospect of the first YoY quarterly demand drop since 2009 and waiting on OPEC+ as the market debated whether a proposed 1.5M bpd cut would be enough.

primary_cause: Margin compression fears from lower short rates and plunging yields after Fed emergency 50bp cut. 10-year yield hit record low ~0.9%
secondary_factors: Broad risk-off sentiment across brokers and asset gatherers. Reuters noted S&P banks index fell 4.7% on Mar 6 after brutal week
store_description: Schwab's decline is best explained by the market repricing its net-interest-income outlook after the emergency rate cut. For a broker-bank hybrid like Schwab near-zero-rate fears were especially damaging and the simultaneous flight to Treasuries made the earnings-pressure signal worse.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 3 Thermo Fisher agreed to buy Qiagen for about $11.5B including debt. Deal-related pressure layered on market selloff
secondary_factors: Broad healthcare-equipment de-risking with market down sharply. Investors often punish acquirers initially on financing integration and price concerns
store_description: The clearest stock-specific item was Thermo Fisher's large Qiagen acquisition announced Mar 3. Even though strategically it made sense investors often punish acquirers initially because of financing integration and price concerns and that was exacerbated by the March 5 COVID-driven risk-off tape.

primary_cause: No strong TMUS-specific headline. Broad market selloff with Sprint merger still pending closing Apr 1
secondary_factors: Merger uncertainty over timing and integration plus general equity de-risking
store_description: This looks mostly tape-driven. No persuasive evidence of a fresh March 2-5 company-specific negative catalyst. The Sprint deal was known and the biggest milestone did not arrive until April 1 so the March 5 move appears mostly market-driven with some merger-risk overhang.

primary_cause: No definitive Tesla-specific negative announcement. High-beta growth-stock selloff amid renewed COVID panic
secondary_factors: Investor concerns about supply-chain and demand disruption for autos. Later COVID factory shutdown news came Mar 19 not before this drop
store_description: Tesla had been an extremely volatile momentum name so on a day when the Nasdaq sold off and investors rushed out of cyclicals and high-beta equities TSLA was vulnerable even without a fresh company-specific bombshell. No convincing prior-3-day Tesla headline found.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and industrial-demand fears tied to COVID. TXN is bellwether for industrial and analog chip demand
secondary_factors: General market de-risking. Apple Feb warning had reinforced broader tech hardware supply and demand scare
store_description: Texas Instruments traded like a macro bellwether. If investors expected weaker factory activity lower auto production and softer electronics demand TXN would get marked down quickly. No fresh TXN-only catalyst in the prior 3 days.

primary_cause: Early COVID demand fears for ridesharing and mobility. Core business directly exposed to reduced airport trips commuting and nightlife
secondary_factors: Persistent AB5 contractor-model overhang and general risk-off pressure on unprofitable growth names. Travel-demand warnings intensifying rapidly
store_description: Uber's move looks more fundamental than some software names because its core business was directly exposed to reduced airport trips commuting and nightlife. By March 5 investors were already bracing for a severe travel slowdown and Uber's still-fragile profitability profile made the stock particularly sensitive.

primary_cause: Lower-rate and flatter-net-interest-margin fears after Fed emergency cut. 10-year yield at record low ~0.9%
secondary_factors: Recession and credit-loss fears as COVID spread. Reuters said drop in Treasury yields weighed heavily on financial companies
store_description: For US Bancorp the market was repricing both earnings power and credit quality at once. The March 3 emergency cut hit asset yields immediately and the renewed March 5 panic added fears around consumer and commercial loan losses.

primary_cause: Fears of weaker cross-border transaction volumes as travel froze. Travel associations warning about sharp decline in international travel to U.S.
secondary_factors: General consumer-spending anxiety and broad market weakness
store_description: Visa usually holds up better than banks but its highest-margin business is tied to cross-border volume and that was exactly the category investors were starting to discount hard. The stock move fits a travel-spending shock more than any Visa-specific corporate headline.

primary_cause: Rate-cut and yield-collapse damage to bank earnings outlook. Wells already a weaker bank story entering COVID shock
secondary_factors: Recession and credit-quality fears. Reuters explicitly tied drop in yields to weakness in financial shares
store_description: Wells was already a weaker bank story entering the COVID shock so a sudden compression in rates and rising loss expectations hit it especially hard. No new company-specific Wells headline in the prior 3 days that explains the move better than the macro banking setup.

primary_cause: COVID fears around away-from-home beverage consumption including restaurants theaters sports venues and travel corridors
secondary_factors: General market selloff and reduced event and travel activity. Reuters later quantified away-from-home channels as about half of Coca-Cola revenue
store_description: Coca-Cola is defensive in many environments but this was the wrong kind of shock — one that threatened stadiums cinemas restaurants and travel corridors. No new company-specific announcement in the prior 3 days so the drop looks like investors repricing its on-premise exposure.

primary_cause: Smartphone supply-chain and demand fears from COVID. Apple Feb warning was major read-through for handset-linked suppliers
secondary_factors: Broader semiconductor selloff and Apple ecosystem read-through
store_description: Qualcomm's decline looks mostly like a handset-cycle de-rating as investors worried that factory disruptions and weaker consumer demand would delay unit growth. No convincing company-specific negative catalyst in the prior 3 days.

primary_cause: Lower-rate pressure on net interest income after Fed emergency 50bp cut. 10-year yield at record low ~0.9%
secondary_factors: Rising expected credit losses and broad equity-market risk aversion. Reuters directly linked yield drop to heavy weakness in financial shares
store_description: Even though JPMorgan was among the stronger large banks fundamentally the market was discounting a much weaker 2020 earnings picture almost overnight. Falling rates and rising recession risk created a one-two punch for bank valuation multiples and earnings estimates.

primary_cause: Look-through exposure to cyclical holdings being repriced for COVID including airlines financials industrials and Apple
secondary_factors: Insurance and industrial operations also faced macro uncertainty. Bank holdings hurt by rate shock
store_description: Berkshire traded like a diversified cyclical portfolio not because of a fresh announcement. Investors were marking down its public equity book and implicitly its operating subsidiaries as recession fears accelerated. No new Berkshire-specific corporate headline in the prior 3 days.

primary_cause: Aerospace and industrial demand fears from COVID as travel and manufacturing activity weakened
secondary_factors: General cyclical de-risking and exposure to Boeing and airline activity. Reuters later showed aerospace business was major COVID-hit segment
store_description: Honeywell was effectively a macro industrial on this date. With airlines travel demand and factory activity all being repriced lower investors discounted its aerospace and industrial automation earnings power even absent a fresh company-specific event.

primary_cause: No IBM-specific headline. Broad-market weakness and concerns enterprise IT spending could soften if COVID triggered recession
secondary_factors: Rotation out of legacy tech and cyclically exposed large-cap software and services
store_description: For IBM there is not enough evidence for a stock-specific catalyst. This looks like a macro-led de-rating of slower-growth enterprise tech as investors prepared for weaker corporate budgets.

primary_cause: Ongoing reassessment of Feb 18 warning about missing March-quarter guidance due to COVID supply chain and demand damage
secondary_factors: Wider tech hardware selloff and China manufacturing uncertainty. Reuters reported major assembler expected Apple March-quarter orders to fall about 18% YoY
store_description: Apple's March 5 decline was not a new surprise but a continuation of the February 18 warning being repriced into a worsening global outlook. Investors were no longer worried only about Chinese factory disruption but also about end-demand for iPhones and other devices.

primary_cause: No Accenture-specific headline. Macro risk-off and anticipated slowdown in enterprise discretionary spending
secondary_factors: Rotation out of high-multiple services and IT names. Consulting and digital-transformation budgets expected to be delayed
store_description: Accenture tends to trade on corporate spending confidence and by March 5 that confidence was collapsing fast. No more specific company-level cause from the evidence found.

primary_cause: No Adobe-specific headline. Broad software and growth-stock de-risking
secondary_factors: Expected slowdown in enterprise and SMB demand if COVID spread worsened. Multiple compression in premium software names
store_description: Adobe was largely a correlation casualty on this date. No credible stock-specific headline in the prior 3 days so the best explanation is multiple compression in premium software names during a renewed market panic.

primary_cause: Semiconductor-sector de-rating on COVID disruption fears. AMD high-beta profile made move larger than some peers
secondary_factors: Supply-chain and demand anxiety as COVID disrupted manufacturing and raised concerns about PCs gaming and broader electronics demand
store_description: AMD traded like a risk-on semiconductor momentum stock so when the market swung risk-off again on March 5 it sold off harder than many large-cap defensives. No better AMD-specific catalyst found inside the prior 3 days.
